edges.description: Loss of CYB5R3 activity impairs reduction of ferric methemoglobin back to oxygen-binding hemoglobin.
Generalized CYB5R3 deficiency across all tissues in type II disease causes neurological involvement beyond the erythrocyte-restricted form.
Without cytochrome b5, the reductase system cannot efficiently reduce methemoglobin, giving a mild form of the same defect.
Loss of cytochrome b5 removes its allosteric stimulation of CYP17A1 17,20-lyase activity.
Deficient androgen synthesis in 46,XY individuals causes undervirilization of the external genitalia.
Inefficient reduction causes chronic ferric methemoglobin accumulation.
Ferric methemoglobin cannot bind oxygen efficiently, causing cyanosis and exertional symptoms.
Deficient erythrocyte cytochrome b5 reductase activity allows oxidized ferric hemoglobin to accumulate in blood, resulting in clinical methemoglobinemia.
Circulating ferric methemoglobin exceeding 1.5 g/dL produces persistent bluish-brown discoloration of skin and mucous membranes.
Chronic methemoglobinemia and reduced oxygen carriage produce bluish discoloration of the lips.
Chronic peripheral cyanosis and nail-bed discoloration are recorded as nail abnormalities in affected individuals.
Diminished functional oxygen-carrying capacity limits oxygen delivery during exertion, causing breathlessness.
Pan-tissue CYB5R3 deficiency produces generalized central nervous system dysfunction in type II disease.
Generalized cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency in type II disease causes early-onset severe progressive developmental delay.
Non-erythroid CYB5R3 deficiency across neural tissues leads to severe intellectual disability in type II patients.
Impaired cerebral growth and frontotemporal brain volume loss in type II CYB5R3 deficiency result in progressive microcephaly.
Generalized CYB5R3 deficiency in type II disease is associated with bilateral hypoplasia of the lentiform and caudate nuclei.
Basal ganglia and extrapyramidal motor involvement in type II disease manifests with athetosis.
Extrapyramidal motor dysfunction in type II disease causes limb dystonia.
Pyramidal motor pathway involvement in type II disease produces spasticity.
